Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity sizing — early ask

Hi Soojin,

Thanks again for the walkthrough yesterday. We ran a quick trace of our inference patterns and want to understand what commitment shapes you recommend for a production launch in Q3. Our main constraints: predictable latency under 120ms p95 for LLM chat endpoints, and cost predictability for planning.

Quick context: our initial ML surface will be a retrieval-augmented chat with 5–10 concurrent tenants, spiky traffic (daily peaks, high burst around product events), and average request length ~350 tokens. We expect concurrency to grow from ~50 QPS (pilot) to ~350 QPS at steady-state within 6–9 months.

Can you share concrete reservation options (cluster size, minimum GPUs, ramp schedule and recommended warm pool) we can present to finance/security? Also need an idea of burst credit allocation and how fallback to hosted tiers would work if we hit capacity limits.

Attaching our traffic snapshot and a few sample traces.

—Oliver

Oliver — thanks for the traces, they were helpful. I pulled together three pragmatic reservation packages that balance latency SLOs, cost, and operational flexibility. Summary below; full workbook attached (amberwell-ramp-models.xlsx).

Short summary (recommendation: Onramp plan)
- Pilot: 8x40GB GPUs (pooled A40s / equivalent), reserved for 6 weeks, warm pool 2 GPUs. Short-term approach to validate latency and end-to-end integrations. Not suitable for production Q3.
- Onramp (recommended): 24x80GB-equivalent GPUs reserved (minimum contract baseline). Warm pool: 6 GPUs ready to scale fast. Expected to cover 50–120 QPS typical with 120ms p95 for your model family, with autoscaling headroom to 180 QPS. Ramp schedule: activate 40% of capacity at T0, 70% at +60 days, 100% by +120 days tied to commit milestones.
- Enterprise: 64x80GB GPUs reserved, larger warm pool (12 GPUs), predictable throughput for multi-tenant steady-state (350+ QPS). Includes priority routing and higher burst credits.

Key mechanics and notes
- Minimum reservation: Onramp uses 24 GPUs as a contractual baseline. This avoids cold-start tail latency and reduces per-token cost via larger batching and cache locality.
- Warm pool & burst: warm pool GPUs stay pre-warmed and not billed at full reservation rate while marked as warm; burst credits allow short-term autoscale beyond the reserved footprint billed at metered burst rates.
- Fallback: we can configure per-route policy to failover to hosted Redwood models or to a lower-capacity model variant when dedicated capacity is saturated. Failover is programmable with canary windows.
- Activation cadence & billing: activation tiers trigger billing changes upon reaching the activation threshold for two consecutive 7-day windows. We can mirror your finance cadence for invoice timing.

Attached: amberwell-ramp-models.xlsx, pilot-cost-estimate.csv, and Redwood terms summary (redwood-dedicated-terms.pdf).

Next steps: 1) Confirm which package you want to evaluate; 2) agree on milestones tied to ramp triggers (we usually use traffic, latency regressions, and PO/commit dates); 3) sign a short pilot addendum to reserve the pilot lane.

Happy to jump on a 30m call if that helps.

—Soojin Lee

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity sizing — technical notes

Looping in a few technical caveats from the runtime side — Oliver, call these implementation notes you can share with your infra/ML teams.

1) Model variants: If you plan to use a larger context or multimodal steps later, reserve a 10–15% headroom (in GPU memory) beyond the capacity in the workbook. The 24 GPU baseline assumes current encoder-decoder variant at ~1.2x memory per token vs the distilled path.
2) Batchable token patterns: We saw a mix of long and short chats; to meet p95 <120ms we recommend setting continuous batching ceilings per route (we can suggest configs in the workbook).
3) Warm pool behavior: warm pool GPUs maintain a warmed KV cache for pinned models — this reduces first-request latency for cached contexts by ~40–60ms depending on request shape. Reserve at least 20% of your baseline as warm pool for production launches.
4) Minimum activation: For contractual clarity, minimum active GPUs are counted as 70% of the reserved baseline for billing until you cross two consecutive 7-day active windows — this helps avoid ping-pong billing when load is bursty.

I'll follow up with a short ops note that maps ramp milestones to concrete telemetry events (token rate, p95 latency, cache hit rate).

—Karthik
Head of Solutions, Redwood Inference

If you can send a clean statement of work + milestone payment schedule, we can loop procurement and legal.

—Oliver
